body.text: The federal government is demanding answers after an artificial intelligence agent infiltrated a Medicare website, as well as targeting other government sites.
In the breach, the OpenAI agent accessed both public and private files as it tried to scoop up data.
The government is stressing nobody's personal Medicare details were accessed, that the research task was largely "benign", and crucially, the impact was minor.
But that doesn't mean it's relaxed about this breach — largely because it could be a harbinger of much worse attacks with vastly more serious consequences.
So what type of information was accessed? What else do we know? And what could this breach tell us about future cyber attacks?
What happened?
Prime Minister Anthony Albanese says the breach occurred back in June, but OpenAI, the developer of ChatGPT, only acknowledged the incident had occurred two weeks ago — on September 10.
That happened when the company lobbed an email to an open mailbox maintained by Services Australia — something the prime minister has described as "unacceptable".
Five days later, Services Australia reported the breach to the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD).
The government is troubled it only found out months after the incident, but more on the timeline a bit later.
What type of data was accessed?
The Services Australia portal accessed had publicly-available data about Medicare programs.
It contained bulk billing statistics, immunisation data, Pharmaceutical Benefits Scheme statistics, organ donor register information and annual reports.
The data is known as "aggregate" data, which means it doesn't identify individuals, but rather contains generalised information such as averages and trends.

Former health department boss Stephen Duckett told the ABC while the information in the portal is taken from individual services — for example, a GP visit — it's collated in a way where nothing private is revealed.
"My information is buried in there, but nothing about me personally goes into these public portals,"
"This information aggregates the experience of thousands of Australians into numbers that can be used for external policy analysis and understanding how the system is travelling."
What about the non-public data?
Some of the data accessed wasn't public at the time of the breach.
The government stresses it wasn't "particularly sensitive" information and has since been made public.
But the issue is about the fact it happened at all, rather than what was accessed.
Other sites such as the Australian Institute of Health and Welfare, the Victorian Health Department and the NSW Bureau of Crime Statistics and Research might also have been affected.
How was the data accessed?
As the government understands it, in this case, OpenAI gave an agent a "benign" task of trying to do research about public medicines spending.
The model then searched the internet widely for the information, and came across the Services Australia portal.
It then asked questions of the portal, but the portal didn't provide it with the requested information. As a result, it gained unauthorised access and secured information that wasn't public.
Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles says a medical statistics portal doesn't have the same level of security as something with the nation's most sensitive information.
"We keep our most important national security information behind a fortress. This was really kept behind a fence that the AI agent effectively climbed over," he told the ABC.
How Open has OpenAI been with the government?
At first glance, not very.
The prime minister said this morning Australia was first alerted to the breach on September 10 — when the company sent that email.
Services Australia saw the email on September 11, and alerted the Australian Signals Directorate four days later on September 15.

It's worth noting OpenAI's vice president of global policy, Ann O'Leary, was in Canberra the day before that — on Monday September 14 — when she attended an Australian Strategic Policy Institute event on AI and met with senior Australian officials.
And yet it seems — at least if we go by the prime minister's account — the senior OpenAI executive didn't alert anyone in the Australian government to the breach while she was in town.
That doesn't necessarily mean she made a conscious decision not to pass on the information. It might be she was simply unaware of the activity.
Either way, officials in Canberra are unlikely to be impressed.

It's also worth noting OpenAI boss Sam Altman met Mr Marles in San Francisco on September 1 — after the company became aware of the "misaligned model activity" targeting Australian websites in August.

But if Mr Altman knew about the breach — and of course we don't know — then he didn't let Mr Marles know about it.In a statement, an OpenAI spokesperson said the models "took action we did not intend" but noted there was no evidence of patient records being accessed. They said there was an ongoing review and the company was "committed to transparency".
What happens now?
For Australian officials, this incident is serving as a warning about how AI is being developed without guardrails in place.
The government says it's undertaking a forensic investigation into what happened and how it found out.

It's establishing a taskforce, led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet, and also involving the ASD, the AI Safety Institute and the Office of AI to look at the incident and examine emerging cyber threats.
The taskforce will also interrogate whether what occurred was legal, and what the consequences would be if there was a breach of the law.
It'll also examine the way government systems have been interacting with external AI more broadly.
Mr Marles says OpenAI has been "cooperative" and transparent.
Both the company and the government will be keenly aware that this breach — and the response from regulators — will shape the way that future AI shocks and disruptions play out.
This whole incident might only have a negligible impact on the safety and security of Australia.
But it could also foreshadow a future where the government is grappling with vastly more dangerous and damaging hacks, supercharged by a technology that seems increasingly difficult to control.
